prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form that made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I keep a one-part prize for B027 and have not changed my configuration since round 1. After reading all six statements, the case still rests on the science and not on the unanimous opening ranks. The arc is complete and independently replicated: proglucagon processing and the incretin effect (Holst), the proglucagon-derived peptides and receptor biology (Drucker), identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) form (Mojsov), and then outcome-trial evidence in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. There is a clear change in the field. Maturity is not the issue. The chair is right that the open questions are the third name and the scope of the citation. I resolve both in favour of a physiology-anchored citation naming Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The citation says 'made possible' treatment, so it ties the discovery to the therapies without crediting drug design that the three named people did not carry out.
statement.case_against: The weakness is attribution. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is disputed and Habener, who is outside the credited names, may have a comparable claim. Nothing supplied lets the committee settle that, and I should not claim more certainty than the record gives. Knudsen's long-acting analogues are what reached patients, so a physiology-only prize can look detached from the clinical change, and a one-part prize leaves no space for B014 or B039 under the three-person cap. I accept both costs. The alternative of naming Knudsen instead of Mojsov would turn the prize toward drug development, and a discovery prize that rests its third name on a disputed priority is still more defensible than one that rests on optimisation of a known peptide.

responses.point: Sandberg moved from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen in her opening trio to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, while calling Mojsov's relative weight the least certain element of the set.
responses.response: I welcome the move, since it means five of us now name the same trio and the disagreement is narrower than my round-1 reply assumed. I share your doubt about Mojsov's weight. Where I would press is on the chair's first question. The committee can defend Mojsov's inclusion on the narrower claim that her work established the active peptide as the insulinotropic form in the relevant physiology, without having to adjudicate the full synthesis priority against Habener. If that narrower claim cannot be supported from the materials, the honest consequence is a less certain third name, not a switch to Knudsen. I therefore hold my position and keep the uncertainty visible.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius argues that choosing Mojsov over Knudsen can be read as favouring early peptide characterization over the drug design that made GLP-1 therapy usable, and keeps B036 as her first alternative.
responses.response: I agree that the reading you describe is the real cost of my configuration, and I do not think it can be argued away. My answer is about what the prize is for. The change in the field is that a gut hormone became a pharmacological target with outcome benefit, and that follows from the physiology and the identification of the active peptide. Analogue engineering is the step that realised it, and I regard it as development built on that discovery. On B036, I still see a thinner discovery component, since TNF biology and antibody engineering lie outside Feldmann and Maini, and the overlap with IL-6 blockade complicates the claim of a single originating paradigm. I rank it below B014 and B039 for a second part, but I accept that this is a matter of degree.

responses.point: As chair, Svenningsson notes that a single GLP-1 part leaves no space for a second achievement, so a strong candidate such as the unfolded protein response would have to wait, and asks in the summary whether a smaller GLP-1 configuration could be paired with another part.
responses.response: I considered the paired option seriously, because B014 is a clean, fully mature two-person discovery. The difficulty is arithmetic and substance. With a three-person cap, pairing B014 (Mori and Walter) would leave one GLP-1 name, and cutting the GLP-1 part to one person would break the arc the committee agrees on and would drop either Holst or Drucker, both core discoverers. That is a worse prize than a single-part B027 with three names. I would rather let B014 wait than weaken the case we agree is strongest. Your point that the UPR is delayed by this choice is fair, and I leave it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Linnarsson leaves the citation scope open between physiology only and acknowledgement of long-acting drug development, and lists CAR-T (B039) as the main non-metabolic alternative while noting the unresolved credit for the original chimeric receptor concept.
responses.response: On the citation I land between your two options. The phrase 'made possible incretin-based treatment' acknowledges the therapeutic outcome without naming drug design or Knudsen, so the citation stays honest about whom it credits. On B039, I agree with your reading of the credit problem and add that Rosenberg's adoptive transfer and TIL work is a different line from the CD19 CAR work of June and Sadelain. The three credited names therefore describe a family of related achievements more than one, and Eshhar's absence makes this harder to defend. I keep B039 as an alternative because of its maturity and clinical weight, but not as a part I would add this year.

responses.point: El Manira warns that choosing the drug developer over a discoverer would turn the prize into a pharmaceutical development prize, while rewarding only the discovery side risks a citation detached from the therapies the public associates with it, and says neither option is clean.
responses.response: I agree with the symmetry you describe, and I take it as a reason to be explicit about the choice and not pretend it is costless. The tie-breaker for me is the criterion that the prize recognises a specific discovery with a discernible change in the field. Of the two errors, omitting the developer of an analogue is the smaller, because the discovery of the hormone's action and its active form is what the later drugs depend on, whereas crediting a developer in place of a discoverer changes the nature of the prize. I would not describe the choice as clean, and I will record that in my uncertainties.

uncertainties: Whether the record supports Mojsov's priority for the active peptide against Habener's claim. I cannot resolve this from the supplied materials and my vote on the third name depends on it.
Whether a citation that omits Knudsen conveys the clinical change adequately, or whether it reads as detached from the drugs.

Whether B014 or B039 would be the better second part in a reconsidered configuration, given that the three-person cap leaves no room beside three GLP-1 names and that B039 has an unresolved credit issue involving Eshhar.
How far the opening unanimity should be discounted as shared exposure to the same candidate dossiers and not as independent confirmation.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal. I overlapped with Ronald Evans on nuclear receptors during my Salk period, but he is not a credited name on the shortlist. I have co-authored with Per Svenningsson (about twenty works) and once with Abdel El Manira on topics unrelated to any shortlisted achievement. Nobody credited in B027, B014 or B039 has a documented connection to me. Institutional membership at Karolinska Institutet establishes no personal tie, and I infer none.
